Tool summary: The search turned up the original post and its Hacker News discussion, but nothing about auth or Stripe specifically.
- The post: Marcin Budkowski's essay "The 100 hour gap between a vibecoded prototype and a working product" describes spending about 100 hours vibecoding a simple app called Cryptosaurus. The first hour produced a working prototype. The rest went to polishing: each iteration took a few minutes of prompting, letting the LLM build, checking the result, and reprompting. (https://kanfa.macbudkowski.com/vibecoding-cryptosaurus)
- HN discussion: The thread (item 47386636) is mostly about whether the LLM speeds up the work. One commenter argues that the improvement drops to about 2-3x because of back-and-forth and code review, and that long-running tests remain a bottleneck. Another puts the gap in terms of effort: you get 80% done in 20% of the time, so the remaining work is what's expensive. (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47386636)
- Related reports: A SaaStr post about a 47,000-line app makes a similar point about the distance between a demo and something people actually use. (https://saastr.com/how-long-it-really-takes-to-one-shot-an-app-47000-lines-of-code-later/)

Tool x.com title: "'Slopfix' software team charges $10,000 a week to delete AI-generated code bloat — ironically, the team uses AI agents to trim messy repositories by up to 65%"
Tool summary: Slopfix is a three-engineer shop that charges $10,000 for one week of work. It agrees on a deletion target with each client, and ties payment to the share of that target its engineers hit. Its headline example is a project that was reduced from 100,000 lines to 35,000 while maintaining original functionality. Coverage also says the team's cuts can reach up to 65% of a repository.
Process and guarantees: Slopfix reviews a repository at no charge and rejects jobs where its engineers see too little dead weight. Accepted projects get a screen-by-screen and endpoint-by-endpoint inventory that doubles as a regression checklist. Clients receive the reduced repository, the product inventory, a CLAUDE.md instruction file for Claude Code-style agents, lint rules, and continuous integration checks. Slopfix warrants defects for two weeks when its changes break a component that worked before the project.
Client results: I found no named clients, case studies beyond the single 100,000-to-35,000-line example, or independent verification of the outcomes. That example comes from the company's own pitch as reported by press.
Conflicting source: One article (blackwire.world) describes Odra.dev as a site used by extortionists ... demand $10,000 a week to remove it ... I could not corroborate it. Treat that account as unreliable unless confirmed elsewhere.

Tool summary: The McKelvey article is the top result... Quick Answer: No — vibe coding isn't bad, but it's a prototyping tool, not a production tool, and most of the damage happens when people confuse the two. He lists the seven failure types he sees in rescue work (the seven I see rescuing vibe-coded apps are exposed API keys, fake authentication, zero error handling, race conditions, broken payments, unvalidated inputs, and unmaintainable code). He also gives cost figures: a pre-launch review at $200-1,000 versus rescues after launch at $3,000-15,000. The search only returned the article's opening sections.

Tool summary: I didn't find a freelancer blog that gives hour estimates for fixing RLS policies or Stripe webhook auth in a vibe-coded app.
- Vendor turnaround: One rescue service says it diagnoses these apps in 48 hours for a fixed $299 (marketing claim).
- Webhook auth: One audit post reports that every app had at least one edge function with verify_jwt = false. Fix: re-enable JWT checks everywhere except payment webhooks, and verify the Stripe signature inside those functions. No time estimate.
- RLS: common problem is policies written as USING (true). Fix is ownership-scoped policies, plus WITH CHECK (user_id = auth.uid()) on UPDATE policies.
- Webhook failures: common cause is signature check using wrong secret (test vs production).
- Planning: a cleanup playbook puts secrets and auth in a single week of a 30-day plan and warns this is the highest-stakes week. No hours per task.

Another vendor: rebuild warranted when architecture structurally wrong, data model cannot represent real domain, or every change touches ten files. One playbook: refactor for apps with users because rewrite loses implicit product decisions. Counterpoint: "If you're early enough, a rewrite loses you less than you think."
